questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Simpler Form Using a Linear Substitution
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x+y+2}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{z}{z+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{z}{z+2}+1 \\  & =\frac{2z+2}{z+2} \\  & =\frac{2(z+1)}{z+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{2(z+1)}{z+2}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4-\sqrt{y-2x+3}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=y-2x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=y-2x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2 & =4-\sqrt{z+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\sqrt{z+3}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2-\sqrt{z+3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Linear Substitution
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{x+y}-x-y}{x+y}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{{e}^{z}-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{z}}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{{e}^{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-z} & \,⟹\,v=-{e}^{-z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}+\int {e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}-{e}^{-z} & =x+C \\ -{e}^{-z}(z+1) & =x+K \\ {e}^{-z}(z+1) & =C-x\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1)=C-x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1).$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{x-2y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.$
